analysis.one_liner: Requires websites with substantial sexual content to verify every visitor's age before letting them in, backed by fines and prosecution.
analysis.headline: The bill has been introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, with no committee action or floor vote since June 10, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any commercial website or platform where more than a third of the content is sexual material harmful to minors to check the age of every visitor, using digital ID or a third-party verification service, before showing that material. Companies that violate it could face FTC penalties, Justice Department prosecution (including up to five years in prison for executives in aggravated cases), and private lawsuits from individuals. Websites could hire outside age-verification companies to comply, and the bill bars those companies from keeping or selling the collected information.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and children benefit if the bill works as intended: sites with substantial sexual content would have to keep minors out, enforced by the FTC, the Justice Department, and private lawsuits. Companies in the age-verification business would also gain a new compliance market, since the bill expressly allows websites to hire third parties to run the checks.

how_it_helps.text: It requires any website or platform where more than one-third of the material is 'sexual material harmful to minors' to block minors from that content, using digital identification or a commercial age verification system.
It bars covered companies and their verification contractors from retaining or selling any information collected for the age check.

It gives the FTC and the Justice Department enforcement power, allows criminal prosecution of a company's officers with up to five years' imprisonment in serious cases, and lets any individual, including a parent, sue a violating company for damages.
It exempts internet, search, and cloud providers from liability merely for carrying users to a covered site.

analysis.who_pays: Operators of covered websites bear the cost of verifying every visitor's age, and adult users pay in privacy: to view legal material they would have to provide digital identification or pass a verification check, ending anonymous browsing on those sites. The bill does try to limit this by banning verification companies from retaining or selling the collected data.

drawbacks.text: The compliance path is age verification itself: to view legal adult material, every visitor—adult or minor—would hand over digital identification or pass through a verification service, creating identity records around previously anonymous browsing.

The bill relies on a vague 'community standards' definition of sexual material harmful to minors, and gives the FTC the job of deciding when a site crosses the one-third threshold, which invites unpredictable and potentially broad coverage of legal content.

Criminal penalties including up to five years' imprisonment can fall on individual officers and employees of a covered company, not just the company, if 100,000 or more minors access material or the firm profits from a violation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal—keeping young children away from pornography—is widely shared, and the bill strengthens enforcement by adding criminal penalties and lawsuits on top of FTC oversight. But the design carries a real cost: because the compliance method is handing over digital ID or third-party verification, every visitor to a covered site, including adults, would have to prove their age before seeing legal material, and the bill text leaves the details of "digital identification" undefined. The privacy section bars companies from keeping or selling the data, which limits but does not eliminate the concern. On balance it is a serious child-protection proposal with genuine privacy and free-expression tradeoffs that its critics would press hard.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote so far.

narrative.text: Senator Jim Banks introduced the bill on June 10, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action—no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote—appears in the action history.
The bill has one cosponsor, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH), both sponsors being Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost—the bill has simply not moved. If it never advances, the status quo stands: adults browse anonymously online and websites face no federal age-verification mandate.

for.name: Sen. Jim Banks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Republicans and no other members have signed on, so no bipartisan or partisan pattern has emerged yet.

industries.industry: Adult websites and platforms with heavy adult content
industries.note: Sites where more than a third of content is sexual material harmful to minors would have to verify every visitor's age and could face FTC action, criminal prosecution of executives, and lawsuits. Verifying every adult user is technically burdensome and raises privacy concerns that such sites argue would push users to unregulated offshore sites.

The bill expressly allows companies to outsource compliance to third-party verification services, creating a new compliance market these vendors would win. The bill does not cap what they may charge covered sites.

The bill explicitly includes social media platforms as covered entities, so any platform the FTC deems to host substantial harmful sexual material would need age checks. Platforms that keep such content minimal are largely unaffected.

analysis.trajectory: At this stage—two sponsors, no cosponsor list beyond one colleague, and only a committee referral—most bills go no further. It would need a Senate Commerce hearing and markup and then floor time, and similar age-verification proposals have faced free-speech and privacy objections, so its prospects are uncertain.
